title: A log with a hash map: Bitcask
description: The notification service stores the latest delivery status per message. Walk through the life of a Bitcask-style store, from append to restart.

problemStatement.overview:
The simplest storage engine that works well is an append-only log plus an in-memory hash map. Every write goes to the end of a file, and the hash map remembers where each key's latest value lives. This is Bitcask, the default engine in Riak.

The notification service fits it perfectly: millions of writes like `msg-4471 → delivered`, the same keys updated over and over, and lookups that are always by exact key.

The outline follows one store from its first write to a restart. Fill the blocks. Traps describe other engines or break the append-only rule.
problemStatement.yourTask: Order the life of a Bitcask store: write, read, rotate, merge and restart.
yourTaskSteps: Fill each empty block from Unused.
hints: Data files are never edited, only appended to and eventually deleted.
The hash map lives in memory, so it must be rebuilt after a restart.
Only files that are no longer being written can be merged.
problemStatement.moat:
Setter notes, not shown to learners.

Required chain: append-record → update-keydir → one-seek-read → rotate-file → merge-closed → rebuild-keydir.
Optional splice: hint-files on merge-closed → rebuild-keydir.
Five traps.

platformSpec.passMessage: Append, index in memory, read with one seek, rotate, merge, rebuild. That's Bitcask.

pieces.title: Append the record to the active file
pieces.blurb: Write key, value, timestamp and a checksum to the end of the current data file. Sequential writes only.

pieces.title: Point the in-memory hash map at it
pieces.blurb: The keydir maps each key to the file ID, byte offset and size of its latest value. The old entry is simply replaced.

pieces.title: Read with a single disk seek
pieces.blurb: A lookup finds the key in the keydir and reads exactly that many bytes at that offset. Often it's already in the OS page cache.

pieces.title: Close the full file and open a new one
pieces.blurb: When the active file reaches its size limit it becomes read-only, and a fresh active file takes new writes.

pieces.title: Merge closed files
pieces.blurb: Copy only the latest value of each key from the closed files into new files, drop deleted keys, update keydir offsets, then delete the old files.

pieces.title: Write a hint file next to each merged file
pieces.blurb: A hint file lists key → offset without the values, so a restart can rebuild the keydir without reading every value. Faster startup; not required.

pieces.title: On restart, rebuild the keydir
pieces.blurb: The hash map was only in memory. Scan the data files (or their hint files) from oldest to newest to rebuild it before serving reads.

pieces.title: Overwrite the old value at its offset
pieces.blurb: If the key already exists, seek to its old position and write the new value over it.
pieces.trapIfPlaced: Bitcask is append-only. Overwriting breaks crash safety and fails when the new value is longer.

pieces.title: Serve a range query from the hash map
pieces.blurb: Walk the keydir in key order to return every message between msg-4000 and msg-5000.
pieces.trapIfPlaced: A hash map has no key order. Range queries are the main weakness of a hash index.

pieces.title: Delete by erasing the key's bytes
pieces.blurb: To delete a key, find its record in the data file and zero it out.
pieces.trapIfPlaced: Deletes append a tombstone. The old record disappears when the file is merged.

pieces.title: Merge the active file while it's written
pieces.blurb: Include the file currently receiving writes in the merge so every file is compacted at once.
pieces.trapIfPlaced: Only closed, immutable files are merged. The active file is still changing.

pieces.title: Sort each file by key during merge
pieces.blurb: While merging, order records by key so files can be searched with binary search.
pieces.trapIfPlaced: Sorting by key is what turns a log into an SSTable. A hash index doesn't need it.
